title: Capstone Part 1: Data Acquisition and EDA
summary: The capstone is where everything comes together into one portfolio-worthy project, and Part 1 focuses on the foundation that determines whether the whole project succeeds: understanding and preparing your data. You start by acquiring your chosen data
content:
# Capstone Part 1: Data Acquisition and EDA

##### The three days that saved three weeks

Two students started capstone projects on the same public dataset — five years of daily mandi prices for onions across Maharashtra.

The first loaded the CSV and started building features immediately. Three weeks later his model had a mean absolute error of ₹340 per quintal, which sounded reasonable until someone noticed that 11% of his rows had prices in rupees per kilogram rather than per quintal — a hundredfold unit difference that had been silently corrupting every aggregate, every feature and every evaluation from day one.

The second spent three days on exploratory analysis before writing a single feature. She found the unit inconsistency on day one (a histogram with a bimodal shape separated by two orders of magnitude), found that four mandis had name variants splitting their history into fragments, found that missing days clustered around festivals rather than randomly, and found that the seasonal-naive baseline was already strong enough that beating it would be the real challenge.

Her model shipped in two weeks and it worked.

Part 1 of your capstone is the foundation, and the temptation to rush it is exactly proportional to how much it will cost you later.

##### Acquiring and loading

Start by getting the data into a form you can trust, and record where it came from.

```python
import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path
import hashlib, json, datetime

RAW = Path("data/raw"); RAW.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

def record_provenance(path: Path, source_url: str, notes: str = "") -> dict:
    """Log where the data came from — you WILL need this in three weeks."""
    h = hashlib.sha256(path.read_bytes()).hexdigest()[:16]
    meta = {
        "file": path.name,
        "source": source_url,
        "downloaded_at": datetime.datetime.now().isoformat(),
        "sha256_prefix": h,
        "size_mb": round(path.stat().st_size / 1e6, 2),
        "notes": notes,
    }
    Path("data/raw/provenance.json").write_text(json.dumps(meta, indent=2))
    return meta

df = pd.read_csv(
    RAW / "mandi_prices.csv",
    encoding="utf-8",                                    # Devanagari, ₹
    parse_dates=["arrival_date"],
    dayfirst=True,                                       # DD/MM in Indian data
    dtype={"market_code": str, "district_code": str},    # preserve leading zeros
    na_values=["", "NA", "N/A", "-", "NULL", "#N/A", "nil"],
    thousands=",",
)
print(df.shape)
```

Three arguments doing real work there. `dayfirst=True` because `03/04/2026` is 3 April in India and Pandas will otherwise guess inconsistently across a single file. `dtype=str` on codes because a market code of `0421` becomes `421` as an integer. And an explicit `na_values` list because real exports use half a dozen different markers for missing.

**Never edit the raw file.** Everything writes to `data/processed/`. That discipline means you can always start again after discovering, on day nine, that a cleaning decision was wrong.

##### The structured EDA

Work through this in order. Resist jumping to the interesting-looking chart.

**Step 0 — context.** Before any code, write a one-line definition of every column. Mark the ones you had to guess; those are the questions to ask, or the columns to treat with suspicion.

```python
data_dictionary = {
    "arrival_date": "Date produce arrived at the mandi",
    "market": "Mandi name — FREE TEXT, expect variants",
    "commodity": "Crop name",
    "variety": "Sub-variety — 40% missing, unclear if optional or unrecorded",
    "arrivals_tonnes": "Quantity arrived",
    "min_price": "Lowest transacted price — UNIT UNCLEAR, verify",
    "modal_price": "Most common transacted price — the target",
    "max_price": "Highest transacted price",
}
```

**Step 1 — structure and quality.**

```python
print(df.shape, df.index.is_unique)
print(df.dtypes.value_counts())
print(df.sample(5, random_state=42).T)     # sample, not head — files are often sorted

quality = pd.DataFrame({
    "dtype": df.dtypes,
    "missing_pct": (df.isna().mean() * 100).round(2),
    "unique": df.nunique(),
    "unique_pct": (df.nunique() / len(df) * 100).round(2),
    "top_value": [df[c].value_counts().index[0] if df[c].notna().any() else None
                  for c in df.columns],
    "top_freq_pct": [(df[c].value_counts(normalize=True).iloc[0] * 100).round(1)
                     if df[c].notna().any() else None for c in df.columns],
}).sort_values("missing_pct", ascending=False)
print(quality)

print("exact duplicates:", df.duplicated().sum())
print("duplicate keys:", df.duplicated(subset=["arrival_date", "market",
                                               "commodity"]).sum())
```

Two columns in that table earn their place. `unique_pct` near 100% flags an identifier or free text. `top_freq_pct` near 100% flags a constant column carrying no information.

**Step 2 — univariate.** Every variable, one at a time.

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, seaborn as sns, numpy as np
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")

num_cols = df.select_dtypes("number").columns
n = len(num_cols)
fig, axes = plt.subplots((n + 2) // 3, 3, figsize=(15, 3.5 * ((n + 2) // 3)))
for ax, col in zip(axes.flat, num_cols):
    s = df[col].dropna()
    ax.hist(s, bins=50, color="#4299e1", edgecolor="white")
    ax.axvline(s.median(), color="#38a169", lw=1.5)
    ax.axvline(s.mean(), color="#e53e3e", ls="--", lw=1.5)
    ax.set_title(f"{col}  (skew {s.skew():.2f})", fontsize=10)
for ax in axes.flat[n:]:
    ax.set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout()
```

**This is where the unit bug appears.** A bimodal histogram with two clusters separated by roughly 100× is not a distribution — it is two different units in one column.

```python
# Confirm the suspicion
print(df["modal_price"].describe())
print((df["modal_price"] < 500).mean())        # 11% suspiciously low
low = df[df["modal_price"] < 500]
print(low.groupby("market").size().nlargest(5))   # is it concentrated somewhere?
```

For categoricals, watch cardinality:

```python
for col in df.select_dtypes("object").columns:
    vc = df[col].value_counts()
    print(f"\n{col}: {df[col].nunique()} distinct")
    print(vc.head(8))
    if df[col].nunique() > 50:
        print("  ⚠ high cardinality — check for spelling variants")
```

A `market` column with 340 distinct values covering 12 mandis is the name-variant problem, and finding it now costs an hour instead of invalidating a week of grouped analysis.

**Step 3 — bivariate, especially against the target.**

```python
TARGET = "modal_price"

for col in [c for c in num_cols if c != TARGET][:6]:
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.6))
    axes[0].scatter(df[col], df[TARGET], alpha=0.2, s=8)
    axes[0].set_xlabel(col); axes[0].set_ylabel(TARGET)
    sns.regplot(x=df[col], y=df[TARGET], lowess=True, scatter=False,
                line_kws={"color": "red"}, ax=axes[1])
    axes[1].set_title(f"lowess — is it actually linear?")
    fig.tight_layout()

# Categorical vs target
print(df.groupby("market")[TARGET].agg(["count", "mean", "median", "std"])
        .query("count >= 100").sort_values("median", ascending=False).round(1))
```

The `count >= 100` filter matters. A mandi with four records and an extreme average is noise, and presenting it as a finding is how EDA misleads.

**Step 4 — correlations, and the leakage check.**

```python
corr = df[num_cols].corr()
mask = np.triu(np.ones_like(corr, dtype=bool))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 7))
sns.heatmap(corr, mask=mask, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="coolwarm",
            center=0, vmin=-1, vmax=1, square=True, ax=ax)

# Anything above ~0.95 with the target is a leakage suspect
target_corr = corr[TARGET].drop(TARGET).abs().sort_values(ascending=False)
print(target_corr.head())
for feat, r in target_corr.items():
    if r > 0.95:
        print(f"⚠ {feat} at r={r:.3f} — is this available at prediction time?")
```

In this dataset `min_price` and `max_price` correlate above 0.98 with `modal_price` — and they are recorded at the same time, so they would not be known when forecasting. That is a leakage trap discovered in EDA rather than in production.

**Step 5 — the time dimension**, if your data has one.

```python
daily = df.set_index("arrival_date")[TARGET].resample("D").median()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(13, 10))
daily.plot(ax=axes[0], alpha=0.5, lw=0.8)
daily.rolling(30).mean().plot(ax=axes[0], lw=2, color="red")
axes[0].set_title("Series with 30-day rolling median")

df.groupby(df["arrival_date"].dt.month)[TARGET].median().plot.bar(ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title("Median price by month — seasonality")

df.set_index("arrival_date").resample("ME").size().plot(ax=axes[2])
axes[2].set_title("Records per month — check for coverage gaps")
fig.tight_layout()
```

That third panel is the one people skip and should not. A sudden drop in record count means a data collection change, and any model trained across that boundary is learning an artefact.

##### Cleaning, with decisions documented

Every cleaning action is a judgement. Record it.

```python
cleaning_log = []

def log(action, detail, rows_before, rows_after):
    cleaning_log.append({"action": action, "detail": detail,
                         "rows_before": rows_before, "rows_after": rows_after,
                         "removed": rows_before - rows_after})

n0 = len(df)

# 1. Fix the unit inconsistency
per_kg = df["modal_price"] < 500
df.loc[per_kg, ["min_price", "modal_price", "max_price"]] *= 100
log("unit_fix", f"multiplied {per_kg.sum()} rows by 100 (kg -> quintal)", n0, len(df))

# 2. Normalise market names
df["market"] = df["market"].str.strip().str.title().str.replace(r"\s+", " ", regex=True)
market_map = {"Nashik City": "Nashik", "Nasik": "Nashik", "Lasalgaon (Vinchur)": "Lasalgaon"}
df["market"] = df["market"].replace(market_map)
unmapped = df.loc[~df["market"].isin(CANONICAL_MARKETS), "market"].value_counts()
print("still unmapped:", unmapped.head(10))       # iterate until this is short

# 3. Duplicates — inspect before dropping
dupes = df[df.duplicated(subset=["arrival_date", "market", "commodity"], keep=False)]
print(dupes.sort_values(["market", "arrival_date"]).head(10))
n_before = len(df)
df = df.sort_values("modal_price").drop_duplicates(
    subset=["arrival_date", "market", "commodity"], keep="last")
log("dedupe", "kept the higher price where a mandi reported twice", n_before, len(df))

# 4. Impossible values
n_before = len(df)
df = df[(df["modal_price"] > 0) & (df["modal_price"] < 50_000)
        & (df["min_price"] <= df["modal_price"])
        & (df["modal_price"] <= df["max_price"])]
log("validity", "dropped rows violating min <= modal <= max or out of range",
    n_before, len(df))

# 5. Missing values — decide per column, with a reason
df["arrivals_tonnes"] = df["arrivals_tonnes"].fillna(
    df.groupby("market")["arrivals_tonnes"].transform("median"))
df["arrivals_was_missing"] = df["arrivals_tonnes"].isna().astype(int)  # flag first!

print(pd.DataFrame(cleaning_log))
print(f"\n{n0:,} rows in -> {len(df):,} rows out ({(1-len(df)/n0):.1%} removed)")
```

That log is the deliverable. Anyone reading your analysis needs to know that 4% of rows were removed and why — and you need it yourself when a reviewer asks about a number in week three.

Finish with a validation function that must pass:

```python
def validate(d: pd.DataFrame) -> list[str]:
    problems = []
    if d.duplicated(subset=["arrival_date", "market", "commodity"]).any():
        problems.append("duplicate keys remain")
    if not d["modal_price"].between(1, 50_000).all():
        problems.append("prices out of range")
    if d["arrival_date"].max() > pd.Timestamp.now():
        problems.append("future dates")
    if d[["market", "commodity", "modal_price"]].isna().any().any():
        problems.append("nulls in required columns")
    return problems

issues = validate(df)
print("PASS" if not issues else "FAIL: " + "; ".join(issues))
df.to_parquet("data/processed/mandi_clean.parquet", compression="zstd")
```

##### Documenting findings and hypotheses

EDA that produces no written output was not EDA. Close Part 1 with a structured summary.

```markdown
## Data Understanding — Mandi Price Forecasting

### Dataset
Agmarknet daily onion prices, 12 Maharashtra mandis, Jan 2021 – Jun 2026.
183,402 raw rows → 175,890 after cleaning (4.1% removed).

### Quality issues found
1. **Unit inconsistency.** 11.2% of rows recorded price per kg rather than
   per quintal. Detected via a bimodal histogram; corrected by ×100.
   *Impact if missed: every aggregate and every model would be corrupted.*
2. **Market name variants.** 340 distinct strings covering 12 mandis
   ("Nashik", "Nasik", "Nashik City"). Mapped to canonical names.
3. **Non-random missingness.** Missing days cluster around festivals and
   bandhs, not randomly. Treated as genuine closures, not imputed.
4. **Leakage risk.** `min_price` and `max_price` correlate at r > 0.98 with
   the target and are recorded simultaneously — EXCLUDED from features.
5. **Coverage change.** Two mandis begin reporting only from March 2023;
   restricting the training window or adding a flag is required.

### Key insights
1. Strong annual seasonality — prices peak Oct–Dec (post-monsoon scarcity),
   trough Feb–Apr (harvest arrival). Ratio of peak to trough median: 2.4×.
2. Arrivals and price are inversely related (Spearman −0.61), but the
   relationship is non-linear — it flattens above 800 tonnes.
3. Lasalgaon shows the lowest volatility (CV 0.31) and Pune the highest
   (CV 0.58), likely reflecting Lasalgaon's role as a benchmark market.
4. Day-of-week effects are weak (mandis closed Sundays), but month-end
   shows a small consistent uplift.
5. The 2022 price spike (Sept–Nov) is a genuine supply shock, not an error —
   confirmed against news reports. Should be kept, not treated as an outlier.

### Hypotheses to test in Part 2
H1: Lagged prices (1, 7, 14 days) plus arrivals will beat seasonal naive
    at a 7-day horizon.
H2: Lasalgaon's price leads other mandis by 1–3 days (it is the benchmark
    market) — cross-mandi lag features should help.
H3: Month-of-year plus a monsoon-onset indicator captures most seasonality.

### Open questions
- Is `variety` (40% missing) optional or unrecorded? Affects whether to
  impute or drop.
- Can we obtain rainfall data to join? Would likely improve the seasonal signal.
```

Finding number 5 deserves attention. **Verifying an apparent outlier against external reality** — checking whether the 2022 spike was a real event — is the kind of judgement no automated profiler provides, and it prevents you from deleting your most informative data.

##### Common mistakes

- Building features before EDA and inheriting a silent data bug.
- Only `head()` on a sorted file, seeing an unrepresentative sample.
- Missing a unit inconsistency because the histogram was never plotted.
- Not checking cardinality on free-text columns, so name variants fragment the data.
- Reporting statistics for groups with a handful of records.
- Missing a leakage feature because target correlations were never inspected.
- Deleting outliers that are real events.
- Cleaning without a log, so nobody can audit the decisions.
- Editing raw data in place, losing the ability to start over.
- Producing charts but no written findings.

##### Hands-on

Load your capstone dataset and work through the five EDA steps in order, starting with writing a data dictionary. Produce a quality table, univariate distributions for every numeric column, target relationships for the top features, a correlation matrix with a leakage check, and time-based coverage plots if applicable. Document at least five insights, and for each state whether it is a data-quality issue, a modelling implication, or a business finding.

For the mini-project, complete and commit Part 1: a well-documented notebook covering acquisition with provenance, thorough EDA, cleaning with a logged decision for every action, initial feature ideas, a validation function that passes, and the written findings-and-hypotheses summary above. Save the cleaned data to `data/processed/` and leave `data/raw/` untouched. Commit it to your repository with a meaningful message.

For the assignment, write the data understanding section for your capstone — the dataset description, its quality issues, and the top insights from your EDA. Include at least one finding you verified against something outside the dataset, and at least one open question you would ask a domain expert. Those two elements are what distinguish analysis from data processing.

##### Key takeaways

- Three days of EDA regularly saves three weeks; the unit bug, the name variants and the leakage feature are all found here.
- Work systematically — structure, quality, univariate, bivariate, correlations, time — and resist the interesting chart.
- Sample rather than `head()`, check cardinality on text columns, and filter out tiny groups before reporting rates.
- Log every cleaning decision with counts, keep raw data immutable, and end with a validation function that passes.
- Close with written findings and testable hypotheses — EDA that produces only charts has produced nothing.
